posts.title: Survival estimates and knowing the patient
posts.insight: In one US study of hospice referrals, doctors' survival estimates were accurate about 1 time in 5 and mostly too optimistic, and estimates tended to be less accurate the longer the doctor had known the patient.
posts.angle: Challenge the assumption that the doctor who knows a patient best estimates survival best, using one cohort's association and a later review, then offer three marked-as-judgement habits: give a range, name what would shorten it, ask a colleague.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Christakis and Lamont 2000; White 2016 review) plus clinical interpretation marked as 'Our suggestion' (give a range, name what would shorten it, seek a second view); the remedies are judgement, not tested.

captions.x:
The longer a doctor had known a dying patient, the less accurate the doctor's estimate of survival tended to be, in one US study.

In Chicago, 343 doctors estimated survival for 468 people referred to hospice. Median survival was 24 days. About 20 in 100 estimates were within a third of the true time. 63 in 100 were too optimistic and 17 in 100 too pessimistic.

A review of 42 studies found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care were often inaccurate, and no professional group was consistently better.

Our suggestion: give a range, say what would shorten it, and ask a colleague when you know the patient well.
captions.linkedin:
The longer a doctor had known a dying patient, the less accurate the doctor's estimate of survival tended to be, in one US study.

Christakis and Lamont followed 468 people referred to hospice programmes in Chicago. 343 doctors gave a survival estimate for each person. Median survival was 24 days. Of the estimates:

1. About 20 in 100 were accurate, meaning within a third of the actual survival time.
2. 63 in 100 were too optimistic.
3. 17 in 100 were too pessimistic.

The longer the doctor had known the patient, and the more recently they had last seen them, the less accurate the estimate tended to be. This is an association in one study from around 2000, in one city, so it does not show that knowing a patient causes the error.

A later systematic review of 42 studies found that clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care were often inaccurate, and that no group of clinicians was consistently more accurate than another.

Our suggestion is a judgement, not a tested remedy. Give a range rather than a single figure. Say which signs would shorten it. Ask a colleague's view when you know the patient well.

posts.title: A fan, and oxygen only when it helps
posts.insight: In a small trial a hand-held fan on the face eased breathlessness more than the fan on the legs, and in people whose blood oxygen was not low, oxygen eased breathlessness no more than room air.
posts.angle: Offer a cheap measure to try first and a clearer reason to ask whether oxygen will help a particular person, without claiming the trials cover people with low oxygen.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Galbraith 2010; Abernethy 2010; Campbell 2013) plus a marked suggestion (try a fan first; check whether oxygen helps that person), which is judgement.

captions.x:
Five minutes of air from a hand-held fan on the face eased breathlessness more than the same fan on the legs. This was a small UK trial of 50 people with advanced illness. The effect shown was short-term.

A second trial involved 239 people with serious illness whose blood oxygen was not low. Oxygen through nasal tubes eased breathlessness no more than room air through the same tubes. Both groups felt a little better. That could reflect air flow, expectation or the natural course of the illness.

Our suggestion: try a fan first. If oxygen is tried, check whether it helps that person.
captions.linkedin:
Five minutes of air from a hand-held fan on the face eased breathlessness more than the same fan on the legs. This was a small UK trial of 50 people with advanced illness. Each person tried both, in random order. The effect shown was short-term.

Oxygen is often given for breathlessness. A double-blind trial tested it in 239 people with serious illness whose blood oxygen was not low. Oxygen through nasal tubes eased breathlessness no more than room air through the same tubes. From the start to day 6, morning breathlessness on a 0 to 10 scale fell by 0.9 points with oxygen and 0.7 with room air. That difference was not clear. Both groups felt a little better. This could reflect air flow, expectation or the natural course of the illness, and the trial could not separate them.

Two limits apply. The trial excluded people with low blood oxygen, so it says nothing about them. It was in outpatients, not people who were dying.

A small study looked at 32 people close to death who were not in distress. Switching between oxygen, air and no flow made no difference to breathing distress for most. 3 of the 32 became distressed and went back on oxygen. Oxygen also means tubing and equipment, which some people find hard to live with.

Our suggestion, as a judgement: try a fan first. If oxygen is tried, check whether it helps that person, and stop it if it does not.

posts.title: What the later stages of dementia usually bring
posts.insight: In a US study of care home residents with advanced dementia, most developed an eating problem within 18 months, and residents whose families understood the likely course were much less likely to have hospital-type interventions in their last 3 months.
posts.angle: Give families the usual course of late-stage dementia in numbers, then three questions to put to the care team, so decisions about hospital, drips and tube feeding can be made calmly and early. The suggestion to plan ahead is judgement.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Mitchell 2009, observational) plus ethical and practical judgement marked as 'We think' (families should be told what the later stages usually bring and invited to plan).

captions.x:
About 86 in 100 people with advanced dementia (the late stage) developed an eating problem within 18 months, in a US care home study.

The study followed 323 residents. About 53 in 100 had a fever. About 41 in 100 had pneumonia. About 55 in 100 died.

Among those who died, about 41 in 100 had a hospital transfer, emergency visit, drip or tube feeding in their last 3 months. Those whose families understood the likely course were much less likely to have these. The study does not show that explaining the course made the difference.

You can ask the care team what the later stages usually bring. You can ask whether hospital would help, and what will be done for comfort either way.
captions.linkedin:
About 86 in 100 people with advanced dementia (the late stage) developed an eating problem within 18 months, in a US care home study.

Mitchell and colleagues followed 323 care home residents with advanced dementia in the Boston area for 18 months. Over that time:

1. About 86 in 100 developed an eating problem.
2. About 53 in 100 had a fever.
3. About 41 in 100 had pneumonia.
4. About 55 in 100 died.

Among those who died, about 41 in 100 had a hospital transfer, emergency visit, drip or tube feeding in their last 3 months. Residents whose families understood the likely course were much less likely to have these. That is an observational finding. It does not show that explaining the course caused the difference.

The figures come from US care homes and apply to late-stage dementia only.

We think families should be told clearly what the later stages usually bring, and be invited to plan ahead. Three questions you can put to the care team: What usually happens in the later stages? Would going to hospital help? What will be done for comfort either way?

posts.title: Ask, record, review the place of care
posts.insight: Where preferences are recorded, home is the most common choice, but many UK studies never asked or recorded people's views, so the true share is unknown, and about 1 in 5 patients changed their preference as illness progressed.
posts.angle: Revised angle: home usually comes first where people state a preference, so the argument is for asking, recording and reviewing, not for doubting home. A well-planned death in a hospice, hospital or care home should not be counted as a failure (judgement).
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Hoare 2015; Gomes 2013) plus ethical judgement marked as 'We should' (ask, record and review; do not count a planned death elsewhere as a failure).

captions.x:
A review of 61 UK studies found that many people's wishes about where to die were never asked or recorded.

Among the views that were recorded, most chose home. Once the missing views are counted, nobody knows what share of people prefer home. Where people were asked, such as in a hospice or at home, was linked with the place they named.

A larger review of 210 studies from 33 countries agrees that most people who state a preference choose home. In patients, estimates ranged from about 3 in 10 to nearly 9 in 10. In 10 studies, about 1 in 5 patients changed their preference as illness progressed.

We should ask each person, write down the answer and the reasons, and ask again.
captions.linkedin:
A review of 61 UK studies found that many people's wishes about where to die were never asked or recorded.

Hoare and colleagues reviewed UK studies from 2000 to 2015. Among the preferences that were recorded, most people chose home. Once the missing views were counted, it was not known what share of people prefer home. Where people were asked, such as in a hospice or at home, was also linked with the place they said they preferred.

A larger international review covered 210 studies in 33 countries. It agrees that home is the most common stated choice. In the best studies of patients, estimates of preferring home ranged from about 3 in 10 to nearly 9 in 10.

In 10 studies, about 1 in 5 patients changed their preference as illness progressed. Those data came from few studies, mostly of low quality, and the change was not tested for statistical significance.

None of this weakens the case for helping people who choose home. It shows why each person should be asked.

We should ask each person where they would like to be cared for and to die, record the reasons, and review the answer as things change. A well-planned death in a hospice, hospital or care home should not be counted as a failure.

posts.title: The rattling breath near death
posts.insight: The rattling breathing that can come in the last days of life is thought to be saliva and mucus collecting in the throat; experts think it is unlikely to distress the person, but some relatives are upset, so an explanation helps.
posts.angle: Separate what has been measured (relatives' distress in interviews; a hospice trial of preventive medicine) from what is inferred (the dying person's comfort), say that evidence for treating an established rattle is lacking, and give two things a relative can ask for.
posts.position_basis: empirical findings from interviews, a Cochrane review, a scoping review and a trial, with the dying person's comfort stated as expert consensus and not measured; the advice to ask for an explanation is a practical suggestion.

captions.x:
The rattling breathing that can come in the last days of life is thought to be saliva and mucus. They collect in the throat when a person can no longer cough or swallow them away. That is the presumed cause. It has not been shown directly.

Experts generally agree the sound is unlikely to distress the dying person. This has not been measured well. Some relatives are upset by it, especially when they think the person is choking or drowning. Others are not. Some see it as a sign that death is close.

Changing the person's position is a usual first step. There is little trial evidence that medicines reduce the sound once it has started. Relatives need time and explanation.

If you hear it, ask the nurse to explain what it is.
captions.linkedin:
The rattling breathing that can come in the last days of life is thought to be saliva and mucus. They collect in the throat when a person can no longer cough or swallow them away. Some call it the death rattle. That is the presumed cause, and it has not been shown directly.

Experts generally agree the sound is unlikely to distress the dying person. This has not been measured well.

Relatives react differently. In a UK interview study of 25 bereaved relatives, 17 had heard the sound. 10 of them were distressed by it and 7 were not. Relatives were distressed when they thought the person might be choking or drowning. Some saw the sound as a useful sign that death was close. These are small interview studies. They show what these relatives said, not how common each reaction is.

Changing the person's position is a usual first step. A Cochrane review found no evidence that any medicine or other measure was better than placebo for treating the sound once it has started. It concluded that relatives need time, explanation and reassurance.

A Dutch hospice trial of 157 dying people tested an injection of hyoscine butylbromide. It was given as soon as dying was recognised, before any rattle. About 13 in 100 developed the rattle, compared with 27 in 100 given placebo. That tested prevention, not treatment. Restlessness was 28 in 100 compared with 23 in 100.

If you hear this sound, ask the nurse to explain what it is and how it is being managed. You can also ask whether changing the person's position could help.

posts.title: Count the carer's hours
posts.insight: In a national survey of bereaved carers in England, people who cared for someone who died of cancer reported a median of about 69 and a half hours of care a week in the last 3 months, and many reported out-of-pocket spending.
posts.angle: Plans for dying at home are usually described in visits and equipment; the largest input reported here is the family's time and money. Put it on the record and end on planning questions about the carer's limits.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Rowland 2017, self-report, cancer only, 28.5% response) plus a marked judgement ('We think a plan for dying at home should ask...').

posts.title: Parkinson's medicines when swallowing stops
posts.insight: For a person with Parkinson's who can no longer swallow, 'stop all oral medicines' is a decision: sudden withdrawal can bring severe stiffness and pain, a rotigotine patch is the most widely used non-oral option (dose approximate, no trials), and dopamine-blocking medicines such as metoclopramide and haloperidol should be checked for on the chart.
posts.angle: Revised angle: the editor's 'convert, not simply stop' is stronger than the evidence, so the post says to decide on purpose, offers the rotigotine route with its limits, and owns the check for dopamine blockers, naming only the two drugs the sources name. No alternative drugs are named.
posts.position_basis: empirical findings and expert-review statements (Beckers 2025 full text; Hewer 2024; Kim 2023 abstracts), with the recommendation to decide on purpose and agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team as clinical interpretation. Evidence is observational and expert opinion; no trials.

captions.x:
When a person with Parkinson's can no longer swallow, 'stop all oral medicines' on the chart stops their Parkinson's medicines too.

Sudden withdrawal can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety and, rarely, a dangerous reaction with high fever. Some people stay comfortable without the medicines near the end of life, so make it a decision: ask what is causing discomfort.

A rotigotine skin patch is the most widely used non-oral option, but no trials show it works at the end of life. Doses are approximate, and too high a dose is linked with confusion, hallucinations and agitation. Agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team.

captions.linkedin:
When a person with Parkinson's can no longer swallow, 'stop all oral medicines' on the chart stops their Parkinson's medicines too. Four points for that decision.

1. Stopping suddenly can harm. Sudden withdrawal can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety and, in rare cases, parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a dangerous reaction with high fever that resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

2. Stopping can still be right. A 2025 practice review notes that some people have good symptom control without the medicines near the end of life. In one study it cites, severe motor symptoms were present in 6 in 100 people in the last 72 hours of life. So ask what is making the person uncomfortable, and decide on purpose rather than by default.

3. A rotigotine skin patch is the most widely used non-oral option, but no trials show it works at the end of life, and the advice rests on case series and expert opinion. The conversion is approximate, about 30 mg of levodopa to 1 mg of rotigotine, and the maximum patch dose of 16 mg a day corresponds to 480 mg of levodopa. Too high a dose is linked with confusion, hallucinations and agitation. In one Australian hospital audit of people with Parkinson's who died, only 7 of 52 eligible people received the recommended dose. Agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team. Apomorphine and subcutaneous levodopa are other non-oral routes that need specialist set-up and may not be available.

4. Check the chart for dopamine blockers. Metoclopramide and haloperidol are listed as contraindicated in Parkinson's. In the same audit, 43 in 100 of the people with Parkinson's were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine blocker and 31 in 100 of those prescriptions were given. Check every anti-sickness, calming and sedative medicine against its dopamine-blocking effect.

posts.title: The surprise question is a prompt, not a forecast
posts.insight: Pooled across 16 studies, the surprise question picked up about 67 in 100 people who died within 6 to 18 months, but only about 37 in 100 of those it flagged died in that window, so most flagged people were still alive.
posts.angle: Revised angle: drop the Gold Standards Framework attribution, keep the 6 to 18 month window, note that the 37 in 100 depends on how many in a group die, and mark 'prompt, not prediction' as judgement.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Downar 2017 meta-analysis; studies at moderate to high risk of bias) plus clinical judgement marked 'Our view' (use it to start conversations, not to forecast or limit treatment).

captions.x:
Most people flagged by the surprise question were still alive 6 to 18 months later, in pooled data from 16 studies.

The question is: 'Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?' Across 11,621 patients, it picked up about 67 in 100 of those who died within 6 to 18 months. Of the people it flagged, about 37 in 100 died in that window. That second figure depends on how many in the group die, so it varies by setting.

It worked less well in illnesses other than cancer, and most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias. The authors judged it a poor to modest predictor.

Our view: use it to start conversations about future care, not to forecast a date or limit treatment.
captions.linkedin:
Most people flagged by the surprise question were still alive 6 to 18 months later, in pooled data from 16 studies.

The surprise question asks: would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months? Downar and colleagues pooled 16 studies (17 cohorts, 11,621 patients) that followed people for death at 6 to 18 months, not strictly a year.

In plain terms:

1. Of 100 people who died in that window, about 67 had been flagged by the question and about 33 had not.
2. Of 100 people flagged, about 37 died in that window and about 63 did not.

The second figure depends on how many people in the group die, so it will be different in a hospice, a ward and a general practice list. The question also worked less well in illnesses other than cancer, and most of the studies had a moderate to high risk of bias. The authors judged it a poor to modest predictor of death.

Our view, which is a judgement: use the question to start conversations and care planning with the person and their family, not to forecast a date or to limit treatment. A flag that is followed by death in the window about 4 times in 10 is a reason to talk, not a reason to label.

posts.title: When grief stays intense
posts.insight: Roughly 1 in 10 bereaved adults develop grief that stays intense and disabling, it appears more common in older groups, and in one US trial of people aged 50 and over a grief-focused therapy helped about 7 in 10 compared with about 3 in 10 with another talking therapy.
posts.angle: Name prolonged grief so that long, heavy grief is not dismissed as private or as depression, and say that a specific therapy has been tested in older adults, without promising availability.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Lundorff 2017 meta-analysis; Shear 2014 trial) plus a practical suggestion to tell a GP and ask what help is available.

captions.x:
Grief that stays intense and disabling has a name: prolonged grief disorder. Pooled studies suggest roughly 1 in 10 adults bereaved by a non-violent death develop it. It appears more common in older groups. The studies differed from each other, so the figure is approximate.

A grief-focused therapy has been tested in older adults. A US trial included 151 people aged 50 and over with complicated grief, a term for long-lasting intense grief. About 7 in 10 improved with grief-focused therapy. About 3 in 10 improved with interpersonal psychotherapy, a talking therapy used for depression. The comparison was with another treatment, not with no treatment.

If your grief is not easing, you can tell your GP and ask what help is available.

The authors advise caution with the figure.

posts.title: Poorer neighbourhoods and hospital deaths
posts.insight: Across high-income countries, people from the most deprived neighbourhoods were more likely than people from the least deprived to die in hospital rather than at home, to have hospital care in their last 3 months, and less likely to receive specialist palliative care.
posts.angle: Report the gradient in words only, say the studies do not show why, and frame the concern as unequal access to specialist support, not hospital death as worse in itself (consistent with the place-of-care post).
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Davies 2019 meta-analysis, observational, modest effects) plus judgement marked 'we should' (report end-of-life care by deprivation and plan to reach the poorest areas).

captions.x:
In high-income countries, people from the most deprived neighbourhoods were more likely to die in hospital than at home. The comparison was with people from the least deprived neighbourhoods.

They were also more likely to have hospital care in their last 3 months. They were less likely to get specialist palliative care. That is care from a team that focuses on symptom relief and support in serious illness. The gap grew at each step up in deprivation.

This comes from a review that combined 112 observational studies, mostly from North America. The differences were modest. The studies do not show why they occur.

A planned hospital death can be right for a person. The concern is unequal access to specialist support. We should report end-of-life care by deprivation.

Davies and colleagues searched for studies of socioeconomic position and healthcare in the last year of life. They found 209 and combined the results of 112 of them, all observational. Compared with the least deprived, people in the most deprived neighbourhoods were:

1. More likely to die in hospital than at home.
2. More likely to receive acute hospital care in the last 3 months of life.
3. Less likely to receive specialist palliative care, meaning care from a team that focuses on symptom relief and support in serious illness.

The gap grew at each step up in area deprivation. The differences were modest and varied between studies, which were mostly from North America. Because the studies are observational, they do not show why the gaps exist.

A planned hospital death can be the right place for a person. The concern is the gap in specialist support.

We should report end-of-life care by deprivation, and plan how to reach people in the poorest areas.

posts.title: Palliative care alongside treatment
posts.insight: Palliative care can run alongside treatment for the illness itself; in one trial in advanced lung cancer, palliative care from the start improved quality of life and fewer people had depressive symptoms, and some people first think it means death and hopelessness.
posts.angle: Revised angle: anchor 'alongside treatment' in the trial design, not the WHO definition; cancer-only evidence; no 'younger people' claim; survival does not lead. Use the interview study only to show that some people first associate the term with death and hopelessness.
posts.position_basis: empirical findings (Temel 2010 RCT; Zimmermann 2016 interviews) plus a practical suggestion to ask whether palliative care would be given alongside current treatment.

captions.x:
Palliative care can run alongside treatment for the illness itself. It is care that focuses on symptoms, support and planning ahead.

A US trial included 151 people with newly diagnosed advanced lung cancer. Palliative care was given alongside cancer treatment from the start. It improved quality of life. At 12 weeks, fewer people had depressive symptoms (16 in 100, compared with 38 in 100). This was one small trial, in lung cancer. It does not show the same benefit in other illnesses.

In Canadian interviews with 48 people with advanced cancer and 23 carers, many first thought palliative care meant death and hopelessness. After receiving it, they described 'ongoing care' that improved their 'quality of living'. The term still carried stigma.

If it is suggested to you, ask whether it would be given alongside your current treatment.

Temel and colleagues randomised 151 people with newly diagnosed advanced (metastatic) non-small-cell lung cancer. One group had early palliative care integrated with standard cancer care. The other had standard cancer care alone. At 12 weeks, the early palliative care group had a better quality of life. Fewer had depressive symptoms (16 in 100 compared with 38 in 100). Limits: this was one small US trial, in one cancer. It does not show the same benefit for other illnesses or for older people with other conditions.

Why ask? A Canadian interview study involved 48 people with advanced cancer and 23 carers. Their first impressions of palliative care were of death and hopelessness. That led to fear and avoidance, and these impressions often came from conversations with health professionals. After receiving early palliative care, participants described it as 'ongoing care' that improved their 'quality of living'. They still felt the term carried stigma. This is a small qualitative study. It shows what these people said, not how common the view is.

If palliative care is suggested to you or to someone you care for, you can ask whether it would be given alongside the current treatment. You can also ask what it would add.

posts.title: CPR on television and in hospital
posts.insight: In 1990s US television dramas about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital, while in UK hospital audit data fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR by the hospital team did, and about 1 in 10 for the most common kind of arrest.
posts.angle: Set television survival and real survival to hospital discharge side by side (matching the outcome), say the figures cover adults of all ages and vary by type of arrest and hospital, and invite people to ask for the figures that fit their own situation without steering older people as a group.
posts.position_basis: empirical findings (Diem 1996; Nolan 2014 audit), plus a practical suggestion to ask a doctor what CPR is likely to achieve for the person; the post takes no position for or against CPR.

captions.x:
On US television medical dramas in the 1990s, about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital. CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) means pressing on the chest, sometimes with shocks and breaths, to try to restart a heart that has stopped.

UK audit data covered 22,628 adults in 144 hospitals. Fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR by the hospital team survived to leave hospital (18.4%). For the most common kind of heart stop, about 1 in 10 did. The figures cover adults of all ages and varied between hospitals. The TV patients were mostly young people with injuries.

This post argues neither for nor against CPR. You can ask your doctor what CPR is likely to achieve for you, or for the person you care for.

On US television medical dramas in the 1990s, about 2 in 3 people given CPR appeared to survive to leave hospital.

CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) means pressing on the chest, sometimes with shocks and breaths, to try to restart a heart that has stopped.

Diem and colleagues watched 97 episodes of three US programmes in 1994 and 1995. CPR was shown 60 times, and 67% of the people given it appeared to survive to leave hospital. The patients shown were mostly young people with injuries. A later study of two US dramas in 2010 and 2011 found about 7 in 10 survived the CPR itself. That is an earlier point than leaving hospital, so it is not directly comparable.

In the UK National Cardiac Arrest Audit, 22,628 adults in 144 hospitals were given CPR by the hospital team. Fewer than 1 in 5 (18.4%) survived to leave hospital. The most common kind of heart stop, in about 7 in 10 arrests, had survival of about 1 in 10. The less common kind that can be treated with a shock, in about 1 in 6 arrests, had survival of about 5 in 10. Survival varied substantially between hospitals. The figures are unadjusted and cover adults of all ages. The data are now more than a decade old.

These are averages, not predictions for any one person. This post argues neither for nor against CPR. You can ask your doctor what CPR is likely to achieve for you, or for the person you care for, rather than relying on television.
